paragraphs: BOLD investigates whether deep networks can be trained directly with Boolean weights or activations. Existing quantized and binary training methods often keep full-precision weights behind the scenes. They also approximate how gradients pass through discretization, which can reduce accuracy while leaving training computationally expensive.

The paper introduces Boolean variation as a mathematical basis for training within the Boolean domain. This replaces reliance on gradient descent over hidden real-valued weights with a training principle suited to Boolean neurons. The authors examine convergence and evaluate computational complexity while accounting for chip architecture, memory hierarchy, data movement, and arithmetic precision.

Experiments report accuracy matching a full-precision baseline on ImageNet classification and results exceeding the stated state of the art in semantic segmentation. The paper also reports notable results in image super-resolution and transformer-based language understanding, alongside substantial energy reductions during training and inference. These findings support direct Boolean training as a way to reduce computation while retaining strong performance on the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2024-bold-boolean-logic-deep-lea.tldr: BOLD introduces direct Boolean-domain neural-network training and reports strong task performance with lower training and inference energy consumption.

paragraphs: DART-Eval examines whether DNA language models deliver useful capabilities for regulatory DNA: non-coding sequences involved in controlling gene activity. These models aim to learn reusable representations from DNA, but the authors argue that existing benchmarks do not adequately test this important class of biological applications.

The benchmark covers discovering functional sequence features, predicting regulatory activity specific to a cell type, and predicting how genetic variants would change that activity. It evaluates models in zero-shot, probed, and fine-tuned settings. Comparing these settings against contemporary models built from scratch helps assess how effectively pretrained DNA representations support the targeted tasks.

The evaluated DNA language models perform inconsistently and provide no compelling improvement over alternative baselines on most tasks, despite requiring substantially more computation. This finding qualifies their practical promise for the regulatory applications tested. The paper also discusses modeling, data curation, and evaluation strategies that may help future models, making the benchmark both an assessment of current capabilities and a basis for measuring subsequent progress.
neurips-2024-dart-eval-a-comprehensive-d.tldr: DART-Eval finds that current DNA language models offer inconsistent benefits on regulatory DNA tasks despite substantially higher computational requirements.

paragraphs: Confounding complicates causal inference because relationships between variables may reflect influences beyond the causal relationship being studied. Many existing methods assume that all relevant confounding variables are observed. Others impose strong mathematical assumptions on how the data were generated to make hidden confounding identifiable.

This paper develops an approach that relaxes causal sufficiency and parametric assumptions by using causal mechanism shifts and data that are not independently and identically distributed. It considers multiple definitions of confounding rather than treating every question as the same measurement problem. Its methods address detecting confounding among variables, distinguishing observed from unobserved contributions, and comparing the strength of confounding across different variable sets.

The authors also describe desirable properties for a confounding measure and construct measures that satisfy them. Their empirical results support the usefulness of these measures. The contribution therefore goes beyond flagging whether confounding might exist: it provides a structured way to investigate its sources and relative magnitude under the proposed approach.
neurips-2024-detecting-and-measuring-con.tldr: The paper uses causal mechanism shifts to develop measures for detecting, separating, and comparing observed and hidden confounding effects.

paragraphs: Improving fairness with a fixed dataset can come at the expense of accuracy. This paper investigates whether selectively acquiring additional training examples can improve that tradeoff. Its objective is to reduce disparities between demographic groups while preserving predictive accuracy, rather than treating the existing dataset as an unchangeable resource.

The proposed algorithm scores candidate examples by their estimated influence on both fairness and accuracy, measured using a validation dataset. It then chooses a subset for training. Group annotations are needed only for a small validation set, so the method avoids requiring sensitive demographic labels throughout the training data while still using group information to guide acquisition.

The authors theoretically examine when additional data can improve fairness without harming accuracy and establish the possibility of their approach for risk disparity. They also provide bounds connecting generalization error and disparity. Experiments on real-world data support the algorithm’s effectiveness. The results support targeted data acquisition as a promising route to better fairness–accuracy tradeoffs, rather than establishing that every acquisition improves both objectives.
neurips-2024-fairness-without-harm-an-in.tldr: Influence-guided data selection aims to improve group fairness without reducing accuracy, using demographic annotations only on a small validation set.

paragraphs: Model editing corrects errors in a deployed network when retraining resources or access to training data are limited. Graph neural networks create a particular challenge because they aggregate information across neighboring nodes. An update intended to fix one node can therefore unintentionally change predictions elsewhere in the graph.

The authors observe substantial disagreement between the loss gradient for a target node and gradients associated with training nodes. In their analysis, directly fine-tuning on the target can consequently degrade training-node performance. Their method, Gradient Rewiring for Editable graph neural network training, stores an anchor gradient computed from the training-node loss and uses it to modify the target-node update.

The anchor supplies information about preserving existing predictions while the target gradient supplies the desired correction. Experiments across graph datasets, model architectures, and multiple editing situations demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is a gradient-based mechanism for making localized corrections more compatible with maintaining broader model behavior, addressing the interference that arises when graph predictions share information.
neurips-2024-gradient-rewiring-for-edita.tldr: GRE adjusts target-node editing gradients using a stored training gradient to help correct graph predictions while preserving other performance.

paragraphs: Integer programming solvers often use branch-and-cut, which combines a search tree with additional constraints called cutting planes. Good cuts shrink the search space and can reduce the size of that tree. Choosing effective cuts is therefore central to making these optimization methods efficient for a particular population of problems.

This paper learns which cut generating function to use, extending earlier work that selected cuts from parameterized families. A cut generating function can produce a broad range of constraints, including generalizations of Gomory Mixed-Integer cuts. The authors derive sample complexity bounds for learning an effective function from certain parameterized families for any specified distribution of problem instances.

These bounds characterize how much data is needed to support effective distribution-specific selection. Experiments show that learned functions can outperform Gomory Mixed-Integer cuts on certain distributions, so the reported advantage is not universal across instances. The paper also investigates the sample complexity of neural networks that choose a function separately for each instance, connecting fixed selection rules with more adaptive choices.
neurips-2024-learning-cut-generating-fun.tldr: The paper gives learning guarantees for selecting cut generating functions and shows that learned choices can outperform standard cuts on certain problem distributions.

paragraphs: A multimodal model can be evaluated without task-specific training even when its pretraining data already contain the concepts being tested. This paper examines how much such concept exposure contributes to apparent zero-shot performance. It studies the relationship between concept frequency in pretraining data and downstream classification or image-generation performance.

The investigation covers 34 models and five standard pretraining datasets. Across these evaluations, performance follows a log-linear trend: linear improvements correspond to exponentially larger amounts of relevant training data. The authors report that this pattern persists when controlling for similarity between individual pretraining and evaluation samples and when testing on purely synthetic data distributions.

The study also introduces Let it Wag!, a benchmark containing long-tailed data selected using the analysis. Evaluated multimodal models perform poorly on it. Together, these empirical findings challenge interpretations of zero-shot evaluation as evidence of strong generalization to infrequently encountered concepts. They identify concept exposure as a major factor in the tested models’ performance and highlight the sample inefficiency of the observed scaling relationship.
neurips-2024-no-zero-shot-without-expone.tldr: Across tested multimodal models, zero-shot performance strongly tracks pretraining concept frequency, with linear gains requiring exponentially more data.

paragraphs: Federated learning must often accommodate clients with different computational capabilities. Spectral model sharding addresses this by splitting model parameters into low-rank matrices obtained through singular value decomposition. This gives a basis for distributing smaller pieces of a model for more efficient training on individual devices.

The paper develops two sampling strategies for deciding which spectral components to use. Each follows from a different optimization objective. One produces weight estimates that are unbiased, meaning their average agrees with the original weights. The other targets the squared error between an approximation and the original weights, emphasizing the quality of the reconstructed approximation.

The authors explain how both estimators can fit into the federated learning process and discuss practical issues arising during local training. Experiments on commonly used datasets show that either strategy can improve performance. The contribution is therefore both a principled derivation of sampling rules and an examination of their use in training, with the two objectives offering distinct ways to judge a sampled model representation.
neurips-2024-on-sampling-strategies-for-.tldr: Two optimization-derived sampling strategies improve spectral model sharding by targeting unbiased weights or low squared approximation error.

paragraphs: Bandit problems study repeated decisions where an algorithm must learn while choosing among available actions. Regret measures the resulting shortfall against a comparison strategy. This paper sharpens worst-case regret guarantees for two variants: bandits using expert advice and contextual linear bandits, where decisions depend on feature information.

For expert advice, earlier upper and lower bounds did not match. The paper proves a lower bound of order sqrt(KT log(N/K)), with K arms, N experts, and T rounds. This matches the previously known upper-bound rate for the specified setup in which the player selects an expert before seeing that round’s advice. The order of information and choice is an essential part of this result.

For contextual linear bandits, the authors give an algorithm and a matching lower bound at order sqrt(dT log(K min{1, S/d})), where d is feature dimension and S is context-space size. Matching bounds identify the optimal worst-case rate in the analyzed setting, clarifying how these problem dimensions affect achievable learning performance.
neurips-2024-on-the-minimax-regret-for-c.tldr: The paper establishes matching regret rates for contextual linear bandits and closes a bound gap in a specified expert-advice setting.

paragraphs: An agent interacting with others benefits from anticipating their behavior, especially when their policies are unfamiliar or change over time. Existing opponent-modeling methods can struggle to generalize in these conditions and may behave inconsistently. OMIS combines in-context learning with search performed when a decision is needed.

Its pretrained Transformer contains three in-context components. An actor learns responses to opponent policies, an imitator models opponent actions, and a critic estimates state values. At test time, these components support search that refines the actor’s policy while interacting with unknown, non-stationary opponents. The design connects recognizing another agent’s behavior with evaluating possible responses.

Under assumptions described as reasonable in the abstract, the authors prove convergence in opponent-policy recognition and generalization properties without search. Adding search yields improvement guarantees and supports performance stability. Experiments in competitive, cooperative, and mixed environments show more effective and stable adaptation than the compared approaches. These results support combining pretrained behavioral modeling with decision-time refinement for the evaluated multi-agent settings.
neurips-2024-opponent-modeling-with-in-c.tldr: OMIS combines in-context opponent modeling with decision-time search to improve adaptation and stability against unfamiliar, changing agents.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts pretrained transformers using relatively few trainable parameters, but improved task performance can come with reduced generalization. PACE addresses this through a theoretical connection between generalization, smaller weight-gradient norms, and larger datasets. The goal is to control adaptation while retaining knowledge learned during pretraining.

Directly aligning a fine-tuned model with its pretrained counterpart does not necessarily reduce gradients and can even cause them to explode. PACE instead multiplies adapter features by noise and encourages consistent outputs for the same example under different perturbations. Its analysis shows that this consistency requirement implicitly regularizes gradients and aligns the adapted model with the pretrained model.

Experiments support the proposed theoretical explanation. PACE outperforms existing parameter-efficient methods on the reported visual adaptation tasks, including few-shot learning and domain adaptation. It also improves LoRA on text classification and mathematical reasoning. These findings suggest that controlling sensitivity to perturbed adapter features can improve generalization across the tested adaptation settings while maintaining a parameter-efficient training approach.
neurips-2024-pace-marrying-generalizatio.tldr: PACE encourages consistent predictions under noisy adapter features to regularize gradients and improve parameter-efficient fine-tuning generalization.

paragraphs: This paper studies selection from a stream of individuals arriving over time. Their covariates are available when decisions must be made, but the responses that determine whether they are desirable are unobserved. Selection continues until a user-specified stopping time, potentially within an indefinitely long stream.

The proposed rule uses predictive inference to quantify uncertainty about those unknown responses. It also handles two classes of requirements: individual constraints and interactive constraints involving the selection process or selected collection. The framework includes false selection rate, cost restrictions, and diversity requirements, allowing the selection objective to reflect several practical concerns simultaneously.

The method addresses the two constraint classes sequentially while seeking more preferable samples. Theoretical and numerical results demonstrate its effectiveness at controlling both classes. Its significance is that selection is driven by more than a prediction of desirability: uncertainty and interactions among choices enter the decision rule as well. This connects real-time prediction with the practical requirements that determine whether the resulting selected group is useful.
neurips-2024-real-time-selection-under-g.tldr: The paper proposes an online selection rule that uses prediction uncertainty to control individual and interactive constraints together.

paragraphs: Standard Gaussian processes assume Gaussian observation noise with the same variance across data points. Sparse corrupted observations can violate that assumption. This paper develops a robust Gaussian process that assigns noise levels to individual observations, allowing the model to account for unusually unreliable points within an otherwise useful dataset.

A sequential selection procedure called relevance pursuit infers these noise levels by maximizing the log marginal likelihood. The authors show that a suitable parameterization makes this objective strongly concave in the point-specific noise variances. This mathematical property implies weak submodularity for the associated subset-selection problem, which in turn yields approximation guarantees for the algorithm.

The evaluation compares the model with other approaches on regression and Bayesian optimization tasks. It includes sparse label corruptions that fall within or near the function’s normal range, a setting where corrupted values can resemble plausible observations. The central contribution combines a model aimed at sparse-outlier robustness with an optimization structure that supports formal guarantees; the abstract describes these comparisons without asserting uniform empirical superiority.
neurips-2024-robust-gaussian-processes-v.tldr: Relevance pursuit gives Gaussian processes point-specific noise levels for sparse-outlier robustness, with approximation guarantees derived from the optimization structure.

paragraphs: Polynomial optimization seeks the best value of a polynomial objective, potentially subject to constraints. In many applications, the polynomial also depends on uncertain external parameters. S-SOS extends a sum-of-squares approach to this setting, addressing how global optimization and uncertainty in those parameters can be handled together.

The method constructs a hierarchy of semidefinite programs. These jointly produce strict lower bounds on the global minimum and extract candidates for global minimizers that depend on the parameters. The distinction matters: a bound provides information about the optimum, while an extracted candidate proposes where it may be attained. The authors prove quantitative convergence as the hierarchy’s degree increases.

The paper applies the method to both constrained and unconstrained problems parameterized by random variables. It also introduces sparsity using n-body priors from condensed matter physics. With this structure, S-SOS produces solutions and uncertainty intervals for sensor network localization problems with up to 40 variables and semidefinite matrices larger than 800 by 800, demonstrating the approach on a concrete uncertainty-aware optimization application.
neurips-2024-s-sos-stochastic-sum-of-squ.tldr: S-SOS uses a convergent semidefinite hierarchy to bound polynomial optima and extract candidate solutions under random external parameters.

paragraphs: SAMI trains language models to follow behavioral principles without preference labels or demonstrations. It treats a set of principles as a constitution and iteratively fine-tunes a pretrained model using its own responses. The training objective increases conditional mutual information between constitutions and responses, given dataset queries, encouraging responses to reflect the specified principles.

On dialogue and summarization, the trained mistral-7b wins against its starting model in 66–77% of comparisons. On single-turn dialogue, it also exceeds mistral-7b-instruct, with win rates of 55–57%. SAMI still requires a model to write constitutions. The authors show that constitutions from a weaker instruction-tuned model can align mixtral-8x7b, yielding a 65% summarization win rate.

Further experiments examine diverse summarization principles and scaling to llama3-70b. Reported win rates reach 68% for learned principles and 67% for held-out principles against the base model. These findings demonstrate that self-generated responses and model-written constitutions can support principle-following improvements in the tested settings without human preference supervision.
neurips-2024-self-supervised-alignment-w.tldr: SAMI improves principle-following through self-generated responses and a mutual-information objective, without preference labels or demonstrations.

paragraphs: 3D Gaussian splatting represents scenes with Gaussian elements and supports high-quality, real-time rendering. However, its usual spherical-harmonic appearance representation struggles with sharp, view-dependent effects. These include specular reflections and anisotropic appearance, where the direction of viewing matters in ways that are difficult for the existing representation to capture.

Spec-Gaussian replaces spherical harmonics with an anisotropic spherical Gaussian appearance field for each scene Gaussian. This changes how appearance varies with viewpoint without requiring more 3D Gaussians. The method also uses coarse-to-fine training to improve learning efficiency and eliminate floating artifacts attributed to overfitting in real-world scenes.

The reported experiments show better rendering quality than existing approaches and improved modeling of specular and anisotropic components. The distinction between representation and element count is central: the gains come from a more suitable description of appearance rather than adding more scene elements. The findings extend the demonstrated usefulness of Gaussian splatting to intricate surfaces whose reflections change strongly with viewing direction.
neurips-2024-spec-gaussian-anisotropic-v.tldr: Spec-Gaussian improves view-dependent reflections by replacing spherical harmonics with anisotropic spherical Gaussians without increasing the number of scene Gaussians.

paragraphs: Transformer layers pass information forward, but the representation and routing of that information can be difficult to interpret. This paper studies a mechanism in two language models that selectively inhibits context items. It finds that the mechanism participates in a broader abstraction used across multiple context-retrieval behaviors.

The models write features into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream, which later layers read as communication channels. In GPT-2, a particular three-dimensional subspace indexes positions in lists. When many items crowd this restricted space, copying the correct item becomes difficult, helping explain sensitivity to the order of items in a prompt.

Using singular value decomposition of attention heads, the authors predict previously described interactions between separated heads from weight matrices alone. They also manipulate internal representations and edit weights using the discovered mechanism. On their synthetic Laundry List recall task, these interventions often improve accuracy by over 20%. The results connect an interpretable internal structure to both specific retrieval failures and targeted performance improvements.
neurips-2024-talking-heads-understanding.tldr: The paper identifies low-rank communication channels between transformer layers that explain list-retrieval failures and enable targeted improvements.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a moving object for new viewpoints does not by itself provide a skeleton that can be used to change its pose. This paper tackles both reconstruction and articulation by discovering an object’s skeleton from video. It does so without requiring a predefined template tailored to that object.

The approach combines 3D Gaussian splatting with superpoints to reconstruct dynamic objects. It treats the superpoints as rigid parts, uses cues from this representation to discover a skeleton, and optimizes the result with a kinematic model. An adaptive control strategy prevents redundant superpoints from accumulating, helping manage the representation while learning its articulated structure.

Experiments demonstrate effective and efficient reconstruction of objects that can subsequently be reposed. The paper reports strong visual fidelity and real-time rendering of high-resolution images. Its contribution is to connect a visually detailed dynamic representation with an automatically discovered structure for controlling pose. This makes the reconstructed object useful for changing articulation as well as rendering it from different viewpoints.
neurips-2024-template-free-articulated-g.tldr: The method discovers articulated skeletons from video without object-specific templates, producing reposable Gaussian objects with real-time high-resolution rendering.

paragraphs: LoRA adapters provide economical task adaptation, but their parameters are tied to the base model used during training. Replacing that model normally requires retraining its adapters using the original task data. This is problematic when a service provider hosts the models but cannot retain a client’s proprietary training data.

Trans-LoRA transfers adaptation through synthetic data. A language-model-based generator approximates the data-generating process of an observed subset of task examples. Training on the generated dataset then transfers the adaptation to another model. The observed subset is an important qualification: the abstract describes the method as nearly data-free, rather than requiring no task-data exposure at all.

Across the evaluated tasks, the authors report lossless, and mostly improved, transfer within and between the Llama and Gemma model families. They also demonstrate transfer between different parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods. These results suggest that synthetic task data can preserve useful adaptation when the underlying model changes, reducing dependence on access to the original training collection.
neurips-2024-textit-trans-lora-towards-d.tldr: Trans-LoRA uses synthetic data derived from an observed task subset to transfer adapters across models with no reported performance loss in its evaluations.

paragraphs: Training a language model alternates between forward computation and backward gradient computation. For attention, prior theoretical work had identified parameter regimes where forward evaluation admits almost-linear algorithms and others where truly subquadratic computation would contradict the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, commonly abbreviated SETH.

This paper examines the corresponding backward problem: computing the gradient of the loss for a one-layer attention network. Although gradient computation might appear harder than evaluating attention, the authors establish nearly the same complexity results. Favorable parameter regimes admit nearly linear computation, while the other analyzed regimes carry conditional barriers to truly subquadratic algorithms.

The contribution aligns the theoretical complexity picture for forward and backward attention computation, supporting the paper’s characterization of the training process. The lower-bound claim remains conditional on SETH, and the fast-algorithm claim depends on the parameter regime. Together, the results clarify where theoretical improvements are available and where faster computation would challenge an established complexity hypothesis, rather than reporting a universal practical training-speed improvement.
neurips-2024-the-fine-grained-complexity.tldr: Attention-gradient computation has nearly the same parameter-dependent fast algorithms and SETH-based hardness barriers as forward attention evaluation.

paragraphs: Lane topology reasoning determines relationships between lanes in a driving scene. Existing approaches often improve lane detection while relying on a standard neural predictor to infer these relationships. The paper argues that this underuses lane geometry and makes reasoning vulnerable to shifts in detected lane endpoints.

TopoLogic combines two explicit signals: geometric distance between lanes and similarity between their learned lane queries. Its geometric reasoning reduces the influence of endpoint shifts, while query similarity supplies complementary information in semantic space. Combining these signals creates a more interpretable basis for topology predictions than relying only on a learned mapping from lane queries.

On OpenLane-V2 subsetA, the method reports TOP_ll of 23.9 versus 10.9 and OLS of 44.1 versus 39.8 for existing state-of-the-art methods. The geometric reasoning component can also be inserted into already trained models without retraining, improving their topology reasoning. These findings show that explicitly using lane relationships can strengthen the reasoning stage as well as complement improvements in perception.
neurips-2024-topologic-an-interpretable-.tldr: TopoLogic combines lane geometry and query similarity to improve interpretable lane-connectivity reasoning and reduce sensitivity to endpoint shifts.

paragraphs: Large visual datasets can carry recognizable signatures: neural networks can identify which dataset an image comes from. That observation indicates systematic differences, but does not explain their visual form. This paper develops a framework for identifying the attributes that distinguish datasets and make those differences easier to interpret.

The method applies transformations that expose different types of information, including semantic content, structure, boundaries, color, and frequency. It then assesses how much each information type reflects dataset bias. An additional object-level analysis breaks down semantic differences, while natural-language methods generate detailed, open-ended descriptions of the characteristics associated with each dataset.

The contribution turns dataset distinguishability into a more concrete investigation of what differs between collections. Rather than stopping at a classifier’s ability to recognize a source, the framework seeks explanations in visual attributes and object content. The intended use is to help researchers understand existing pretraining datasets and guide the construction of more diverse and representative ones; the abstract does not claim that this construction goal has already been achieved.
neurips-2024-understanding-bias-in-large.tldr: The paper analyzes visual attributes, objects, and natural-language descriptions to explain the biases distinguishing large image datasets.

paragraphs: Graph learning includes predicting node labels, estimating graph properties, and generating graph-related information. This paper brings node-, edge-, and graph-level tasks into one formulation by expressing classification and regression as conditional generation. The authors provide guarantees supporting the use of diffusion models for these deterministic prediction tasks.

Their Latent Graph Diffusion model first encodes graph structure and features into a latent representation. A diffusion model operates in that space, and a decoder maps the representation back. The framework can generate features at node, edge, and whole-graph levels simultaneously. A specially designed cross-attention mechanism supplies conditioning information when generation must depend on given inputs.

Experiments report state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance across a range of generation and regression tasks. The formulation also encompasses classification, while the abstract’s stated experimental result emphasizes generation and regression. The main significance is a shared modeling approach across different graph-task types and scales, linking the flexibility of conditional generation with tasks normally treated as direct prediction problems.
neurips-2024-unifying-generation-and-pre.tldr: Latent Graph Diffusion unifies graph generation and prediction by formulating tasks across node, edge, and graph levels as conditional generation.

paragraphs: Homography estimation finds an image-to-image geometric mapping used in tasks such as stitching and fusion. Supervised training requires ground-truth mappings, which can be difficult or expensive to collect. Earlier unsupervised methods often work best when images come from the same camera or differ only slightly in lighting.

AltO addresses image pairs from different domains, where both geometry and appearance can differ substantially. It alternates between two optimization phases, one reducing the geometric gap and the other reducing the modality gap. The framework resembles expectation-maximization. It uses Barlow Twins loss for modality differences and introduces Geometry Barlow Twins to address geometric differences.

This division gives the learning process separate ways to handle spatial alignment and cross-domain appearance. The authors demonstrate training on multimodal datasets without ground-truth data and report better performance than other unsupervised methods. AltO also works with different homography-estimator architectures. The results support alternating optimization as a useful framework for learning alignment when appearance differences make same-domain assumptions unsuitable.
neurips-2024-unsupervised-homography-est.tldr: AltO learns homographies without ground-truth mappings by alternating between geometric alignment and reducing cross-modality differences.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an existing dataset rather than gather new experience. When that dataset does not cover behavior relevant to a target policy, its distribution can differ sharply from the policy’s distribution. Without assumptions about this coverage, conventional policy performance is generally infeasible to estimate or optimize.

The paper changes the evaluation objective to a worst-case policy value. It constructively shows that a sample complexity bound of O(epsilon^-2) is achievable without conditions on data support, where epsilon measures policy suboptimality under this new objective. The guarantee therefore concerns the proposed worst-case metric, preserving the distinction from the conventional performance measure.

The new metric generalizes the conventional one, allowing the algorithm to handle standard offline reinforcement-learning tasks without modification. In that setting, the authors describe their bound as a strict improvement over previous bounds under single-policy concentrability and single-policy realizability. The result shows how changing the performance criterion can make learning guarantees possible even when data coverage is unrestricted.
neurips-2024-worst-case-offline-reinforc.tldr: A worst-case policy-value objective enables offline reinforcement-learning guarantees without data-support assumptions, with O(epsilon^-2) sample complexity.
